Changes Summary description and rationale of proposed specialization.
Ever since the inception of the Libraries, Leadership, and Transforming Communities Track (LL TC) in the Masters of Library and Information Studies degree (MLIS), there has only been one course for students to “choose” from in the Public Relations and Advocacy category.
But there has also always been the intention of creating a course that would be added to that category to give students a choice.
LSC 519: Advocacy for Libraries was added to the catalog in AY 2021-22, so this Notice of Change is to add that course as an option in the Public Relations and Advocacy Category so that students can choose from LSC 517: Community Relations for Libraries and LSC 519: Advocacy for Libraries.
We are also seeking to add the optional courses LSC 511 and LSC 512 in one of the categories (Communities and Contexts) since those classes would fulfill the underlying theme of that category in the LL TC track.
Since the MLIS has become an Accelerated Online Program, we also need to remove the COM classes from the track as options because those courses are not available in accelerated online format.

The department voted to remove CHE 570: Research Methods in Engineering as a required course for our PhD program.
CHE 570 is cross-listed with EGR 570.
We intend to continue offering CHE/EGR 570 as a professional elective course for graduate and undergraduate students.
There is college-wide interest in this course and we will be discussing possible options to deliver this course more widely with contributions from other engineering departments.
This could include co-teaching.
Removing CHE 570 as a required course was motivated by three factors.
First, CHE graduate students are gaining much of the knowledge and skills through their research projects with their mentors, through our seminar courses CHE 501 and 502 (required each semester whether for credit or not), and through the university's responsible conduct of research series.
Second, removing this required course is one step we will be taking to reduce our PhD credits from 72 to 64.
In the meantime, the requirement for CHE 570 is replaced in the program of study by an elective.

Third, this course is only required for our PhD program, and consequently it has been under enrolled in comparison to the desired URI course size.
The last time it was offered, for example, there were six students enrolled in the course and the students ranged from �rst year to fourth year in their PhD programs.
Teaching "research methods" provides less value to students who are already in their fourth Ph.D. year of conducting research.
We do not have a recurring critical mass of new, incoming PhD students to enroll in this course regularly.

URI Faculty Senate Research and Creative Activities Committee (RCAC) Report for the Academic Year 2022-2023 Introduction The URI Faculty Senate Research and Creative Activities Committee (RCAC) has been engaged in several important topics over the course of the academic year. These topics included the review of overhead funds on research, the expansion of the committee to better represent the interests of research faculty, and the impact of university policies on the research environment. Review of Overhead Expenditures, Administration, and Policies During the academic year 2022-2023, the URI Faculty Senate Committee on Research and Creative Activities reviewed the research overhead funds collected and spent across the colleges. The committee found that while research expenditures at URI have significantly increased over the past decade, the effective percentage of overhead dollars generated by that research decreased. The graph below shows the trend in the research expenditures at URI over the past decade: Source: URI Institutional Research, John Stringer (2023)

The effective indirect cost collected on research expenditures for FY 2022 was only 19.1% compared to the official rate of 57.5%.
This is a concern that needs attention.
The committee identified several potential reasons why the effective indirect rate is so much smaller than the official rate.
These include the fact that the indirect costs collected from state funds are only 25% and have stayed the same over decades, cost-sharing that may be required on some federal grants, or grant funds from foundations may restrict the percentage of the overhead that could be collected.
Grants for scholarships generally do not provide overhead.
Regardless, the net effect is less overhead dollars available to be returned to the PIs, their departments, and colleges and to support new research initiatives at URI.
During the inspection of the actual indirect cost expenditures, the committee discovered that an associate vice president for facilities was hired with 100% of their salary and fringe being charged to indirect cost, which is out of line with the expectation that overhead for research should be used to support research.

Additionally, there needs to be more transparency on how the division of administration and finance spends the portion of the indirect costs they receive.
By comparison, the division of research is severely underfunded to provide services to the faculty in writing and submitting grant proposals and managing the submission and successful and expeditious establishment of funded grant accounts.
PIs, colleges, and departments report that they are also underfunded to support research activities and investment in growing funded research portfolios.
It is difficult to understand why URI is spending so much on administration and finance from research overhead dollars and not enough on the direct support of the researchers that generate those overhead dollars through their hard work.
The committee encourages a conversation with President Parlange to change the policies for the distribution of overhead.
More favorable overhead distribution to the faculty who generate it will empower the research faculty to be even more productive in grantsmanship and expand the number of faculty engaged in funded research.

These changes will directly align with the URI strategic plan to increase research productivity.
Additionally, the committee spent significant time reviewing how overhead funds on research are collected and spent among colleges at URI.
We found that the current process needs to be standardized across all colleges, and there are discrepancies in how funds are allocated.
For example, some colleges allocate more overhead funds to the principal investigator (PI), while others allocate more to the college or department.
We recommend that the university develop a more transparent process for indirect cost waivers and allocation of overhead funds to ensure

they are used effectively and efficiently to support research efforts.
This process should consider the needs of the PIs, departments, and colleges and the requirements of funding agencies.
Overall, the committee urges the university to prioritize the direct support of research faculty and activities by allocating a higher percentage of overhead funds to support these efforts.
By doing so, URI can maximize its research productivity and achieve greater success in securing external funding.
Expansion of the Committee on Research: The committee considered expanding its membership to better represent the interests and concerns of the research faculty at URI.
We regularly recruit expert researchers to help with the review of grant proposals.
We propose adding non-senators to the Research and Creative Activities Committee.
This expansion will enable the committee to serve the needs of the research community at URI.

Committee on University Research and Engagement (CURE) Charge: The Committee on University Research and Engagement (CURE), an expanded URI Research and Creative Activities Committee, is charged with representing and advocating for the research and and creative activities community at URI.
The committee shall consist of six senators and six non-senator members of the faculty who are actively engaged in research and creative activities.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development shall serve as an ex officio member of the committee.
The committee is responsible for addressing the concerns and needs of the research and creative activities community and recommending policies and practices that will support and enhance research and creative activities at URI.
Membership: The committee shall consist of six senators appointed by the President of the Faculty Senate and six members of the research faculty appointed by the Vice President for Research and Economic Development.
Members shall be selected based on their active engagement in research and creative activities and shall represent a diversity of disciplines and areas of expertise.
